Hello everyone, this is Best Partners, I’m Da Fei. Let’s start with a figure: estimates suggest Amazon is currently developing 44 gigawatts of power capacity in the U.S., more than Google and Meta combined. This scale is staggering in any industry, but what’s truly interesting is what Andy Jassy said on the earnings call: AWS has the potential to reach $ 1 trillion in annual revenue over the next 5 to 10 years. What does that kind of figure actually represent? Based on the current run rate, reaching this goal in five years would require an annual compound. growth of about 40%, or 18%even over ten years. And the starting point for all of this is an existing base of over $ 180 billion. I imagine most people’s first reaction upon hearing this target is similar: they want to understand what exactly it is they’re seeing. Matt Garman, the CEO of AWS, joined Amazon in 2006 and worked on foundational compute services like EC2 early on. His explanation wasn't complex, but it tied a few things together, which I’ll share with you today. First, look at the timeline: at the beginning of this year , Jassy’s expectation was to reach $ 600 billion by around 2036. By the second. quarter, he put the $ 1 trillion figure on the table for the first time. By the third quarter, his tone became very firm , almost like a declaration. They say this isn't just guesswork; they’ve known for 20 years that the cloud opportunity was massive, they just didn’t expect it to reach this scale today. AWS currently has an annualized revenue run rate of $ 108 billion, and it’s still growing at a 39%clip. More importantly, the year-over-year growth rate has climbed for six consecutive quarters. A rising growth rate usually signals one thing: there is something new being poured into the system. His assessment is that this. "something" is AI, but the way AI is having an impact is different from what many people think. For years, the discussion around moving to the cloud focused on saving money—moving servers from your own data centers to the cloud to avoid the hassle of procurement, maintenance, and scaling. This path has been followed for 20 years and is certainly effective, yet a massive amount of workload remains on-premise, with people saying, "My system runs fine , let’s wait until next year’s budget." AI is what changes that judgment. For an agent to do its job, the first thing it needs is visibility into the data. If core operations are still running in. on-premises databases, mainframes, or legacy virtual machine clusters, the agent simply can't reach them. To take a specific scenario: if a company wants to perform analytics, the traditional approach was to move their data warehouse to the cloud and utilize cloud-based analytical tools or platforms like Snowflake or Databricks. Many have taken this step, while others haven't, feeling that on-premises analytics—though limited—are sufficient for their needs. Things are different now; people are starting to wonder if an agent can span across all data and complete tasks in a single go. Cloud engines like QDB can work across different data sources, but the.

prerequisite is that the data must be visible to the agent. If even a single piece of data is locked away in a mainframe, the entire chain is broken. Thus, a new type of pull has emerged— not a pull driven by cost, but a pull driven by capabilities. Garman uses the term "flywheel effect." When customers see AI improve efficiency, open new business lines, and reimagine customer experiences, they realize that unless core workloads are on the cloud, these gains are unreachable. Many might mistakenly assume that the money companies spend on cloud migration is simply shifted from other budgets. Garman disagrees with this view. In his opinion, it’s not about robbing Peter to. pay Paul or shifting savings from A to B ; more often, it’s about creating entirely new businesses and revenue streams. Therefore, he argues that companies refusing to migrate will face genuine existential risks and be left behind by those already on the cloud. He didn’t provide granular numbers on customer structure, noting that while large clients account for a significant portion of growth, the long tail is also expanding. He emphasized that growth isn't just driven by tiny businesses like dental clinics. Those customers are primarily served by partners, who run their own software on AWS. What really. gives him confidence is the breadth; he recently met a group of startups less than six months old in the Bay Area, and on the same customer list are the world's largest banks, healthcare firms , and government agencies. So, both ends of the spectrum are growing. The next issue is very practical: once a business relies heavily on AI, inference becomes a daily expense, and the bill rises alongside usage. There is a term in the industry called "scaling to bankruptcy. " It means the more the business grows, the more the bills spiral out of control , eventually dragging the company down. This is indeed a real issue, and Jassy didn’t dodge it, saying that AWS’s. approach here isn’t to tell customers to use less, but to hand over the control. Customers can set a quota, which automatically stops billing once reached , or set a reminder to be notified when hitting a limit. Inference customers can even set it to automatically downgrade from an expensive model to a cheaper one . These controls might sound trivial, but they are precisely what enterprises look for when making procurement decisions. A large company isn't just worried about overspending $ 10,000; they worry about a specific team, person , or project burning through the budget when no one is watching. Some customers will even specifically request that certain employees have higher limits,. while other individual accounts are capped at $ 100. Regarding capital expenditure, the logic is diversification; external concerns focus on concentration risk—that is, betting massive capital on just a few customers . Jassy’s response is that AWS usage is spread across hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of customers, with signals coming from a very wide range, plus many big clients give five-year consumption commitments, some even reaching 8, 9, or 10 years. These commitments allow capital to be invested ahead of time, but even so, his assessment remains that compute power will continue to be in short supply for years to come, with demand far exceeding supply. There is a.

detail here that well illustrates Amazon’s approach: their principle is to spend money at the last possible moment , because the later you spend, the more information you have, and the more optionality you retain to seize opportunities. In practice, this means breaking down the supply chain by cycle : land must be bought, power contracts signed, and permits secured first—these are all long-cycle items. But servers don't need to be bought now; if planning for 2030, you can buy the land needed for 2030 today, and deal with the servers closer to 2030. He has even calculated the worst-case scenario: if. the judgment is wrong, at worst, the land can be resold, losing some potential appreciation, but land is a durable asset and can definitely be sold . This line of thinking may not be elegant, but it is very practical. So, where exactly does the risk lie in this current wave of compute fever? Jassy’s answer is direct: it’s not a systemic risk, but a localized one, because everyone’s bets are different. He pointed out two categories: the first relies on high-interest debt financing, leaving much smaller room for error in cash flow projections. The second category involves high customer and workload concentration, where the room for error is similarly compressed. For. many new cloud providers, the vast majority of their business consists of ultra-large training clusters. These types of clusters are purchased by only a few customers, and the funding comes from debt. What he means is, this is not the type of business AWS is in. Everyone has data centers and computers, but their business models differ significantly. AWS serves millions of enterprises, startups, SMBs, and government agencies. A large part of this is core computing, including compute clusters, HPC, web hosting, backup storage, and databases—these aren't AI, but they are foundational. As for the AI track, most of it today is. inference. He clearly defined the position of inference: it is a building block within applications. The autocomplete used in emails is inference , the models traders use to judge the next trade are inference, and serving more precise ads is also inference. This means inference is highly decentralized . AWS has huge investments in OpenAI and Anthropic, and they are important partners; but even if usage is concentrated there, the ones actually paying to call inference are the thousands of mid-sized customers running on AWS. So, if one or two companies run into trouble, the demand won't vanish. People will switch models or use open-source ones; the machines are still running. Another, even more counterintuitive judgment is that inference is still in its extremely early stages. There is a frequently cited statistic that only 2%of Americans have paid to use AI, but he feels this stat is a bit misleading. His question is, how many Americans have actually paid for a database? That percentage is likely very low. Yet these people use databases every day, they just don't know it. AI is the same. If you have a Netflix account and are recommended a movie, that is AI at work. Searching for products on Amazon, the search ranking.

also involves AI. Regarding the scale, his judgment is that saying it's at 1% of its final scale is an underestimate— he even suggests it might be less than 1 %. Supporting this judgment is a rule: for every 50%reduction in inference costs, usage grows by an order of magnitude. Today, prices are falling while revenue is rising. Someone asked, where does this money come from? Is it from new budgets, or is it being reallocated? His answer is that it's both. Some are new revenue streams created, and some are substitutions from efficiency gains—for example, not hiring new people and having existing teams do twice the work. The topic then shifted. to the American public's attitude toward data centers. After the midterm elections, a gubernatorial candidate in Texas campaigned on suspending subsidies and won; this is not a small signal. Ben's first reaction is that the industry shouldn't be painted with a broad brush, as some operators ' practices are indeed terrible. He called out a specific group that openly claims to ignore regulations and bypass permits , still building anyway and even taking pride in not cooperating with the community. He says this kind of behavior gives the entire industry a bad name. AWS, however, follows a different approach. From the very beginning, they treat data centers as community projects , not only bringing high-paying jobs to. the area but also minimizing negative impacts, even paying for the power they contribute to the grid. In many communities, they’ve lowered the tax burden, saving every local resident thousands of dollars. Regarding energy, over the past five years, they have been the world's largest creator of new renewable energy, increasing the amount of clean power sent to the grid every day. They thought about the water issue even earlier, pledging to achieve water-positive status annually—meaning they return more water to each community they operate in than they consume. He provided a specific figure: their largest data center currently uses less water than 40 American households, roughly the amount used by a single city. block. Someone added, "Golf courses use more water than that." Garman smiled and said his golfing friends don't like it when he cites that data. Next is what I found to be the most interesting part of the interview: space, the ocean, the desert—where should data centers actually go? Regarding space, his judgment is very straightforward: it is extremely unfeasible economically and practically for the next 10 to 20 years . The story of space data centers sounds beautiful—free solar energy equipment floating in orbit—but launch capabilities can't keep up. He provided a comparison: the world currently doesn't even launch one rocket a day, while AWS installs a GPU into their. server racks every 14 seconds—and that’s just at their company alone. Then there are the physical issues: a GPU rack can weigh a ton; how many could a launch vehicle carry at once, or would they even fit, are big questions. Solar panels produce kilowatts, while a gigawatt-scale data center requires an incredibly massive facility. Because there is no air in space, heat dissipation is actually very difficult. Plus, space is filled with radiation, requiring specialized, much more expensive servers that are hard to repair if they break. He emphasized that these could be solved technically, but that's a long way off. The ocean has similar issues; seawater cooling is an.

advantage, but equipment would float and move, increasing the difficulty, so he believes the ocean isn't very realistic either. Out of the three options, Garman feels the desert is the most feasible, as environmental conditions are relatively better. With natural heat sinks and abundant solar energy, once liquid cooling is applied, it actually becomes easier to manage energy consumption, and undersea cables can solve transmission issues. However, the desert has a side effect: there's nobody there, meaning no one can benefit from the opportunity and employment. People still prefer to live where there are jobs; that is why he keeps emphasizing community value. Let’s talk about the. ecosystem. Inference service providers like Fireworks and Model-F are growing rapidly, are very AI-native, and focus heavily on model fine-tuning. Someone asked him if this is a new cloud market . Jassy doesn't see it that way. In his view, these are more like applications or services built on top of the cloud, which are both complementary to and partially competitive with AWS products , but primarily complementary. Take databases for example: MongoDB and Snowflake are built on AWS, and customers ultimately benefit. The true value of these inference providers lies in helping customers run open-source models effectively, as these models are. difficult to adopt and optimize, requiring specialized knowledge. They have lowered this barrier, so Jassy counts them as part of the partner ecosystem. Does AWS want to control the entire technology stack itself? Jassy’s answer is that they need a position at every layer. At the bottom layer—chips, networking, and data facilities—there are very few participants, essentially just three giants, and that number will likely remain the same because profits are being squeezed. Moving up, the market looks more like an inverted funnel, getting wider and wider, with thousands of companies at the application layer. So they have invested in every layer: self-developed chips and networking equipment at the bottom,. managed databases, storage, and analytics in the middle, and their own applications at the top, such as Connect for customer service, Amazon Q for employees, and Q Developer for developers. He stated quite frankly that even if they don't win the top and bottom layers, if the applications are built on AWS, they are still the winners . Another unconventional move is selling Trainium chips to external parties. Google is also selling TPUs externally. Someone asked Jassy why they don't force customers to use them only on AWS. His answer is that the number of data centers in the world is limited, and AWS cannot handle all the construction. Often, workloads must remain local— perhaps within a country or a government agency—and this is a part of sovereign AI. Take NVIDIA as a comparison: NVIDIA’s chips are not only sold to AWS , Google, and Microsoft, but also to many other places. Today, 85%of workloads still reside on-premises; customers want to train in the cloud, but also keep a portion in their own data centers. That is a business. Compute allocation, however, is a much more fragmented and realistic issue. His answer is that there is no simple solution. They hold regular resource allocation meetings to try to meet demand, but computing power remains.

finite. Sometimes customers want it in two weeks, but they can only offer four . Sometimes they want US East, but they can only offer US West, or even India. If the client accepts, it’s done; if not , they negotiate further. There is one principle he stated clearly: they will not sell 100%of their compute to large AI labs or major tech companies. Even if they could sell out all their accelerators scheduled for 2027, they simply wouldn't do it. Because they need to reserve resources for customers of all sizes, including startups that haven't even been founded yet. Regarding rumors of layoffs and models being taken offline or shelved, he was asked. directly if they intended to give up on proprietary frontier models. Adam's answer was just one sentence: absolutely not. He defined it as a strategic reset . The team needs to hire people to fill in gaps in data organization and infrastructure experience, learning how to drive this at scale. The direction of progress remains unchanged. Customers want AWS to provide first-party frontier models; he wouldn't say more, leaving only the phrase "stay tuned." He spoke most extensively about agent security in the interview. Customer demand is direct : "Give me the tools so I can keep them under control." Because agents are ultimately just tools, they must work. within boundaries, refrain from overstepping, avoid leaking data, and prevent accidents. He believes that what could truly change the landscape is neuro-symbolic AI. Amazon's largest single research investment is what they call automated reasoning. The essence of this is applying mathematical proofs to computer science problems, verifying that a certain proposition is true. He used IAM as an example. When setting up a new permission model in AWS, you can run an access analyzer. It iterates through all permission possibilities within the organization and tells you which rules conflict. If there is a conflict, you must change it; otherwise , the configuration will not be accepted. . If you rely on brute force to calculate these combinations, you would need more computing power than exists on Earth combined. But if you use mathematical proofs instead, you can finish it quickly, and provide a 100% conclusive proof. He also gave a simpler example: for x plus y equals y plus x, brute force is endless, but math can prove it in three steps. The significance of this lies in verifiability. You could have a non-deterministic agent handle insurance claims, letting it solve problems by looking up data itself. At the same time , you must ensure it never violates the. rules you have set. If you can use an automated reasoning agent to place guardrails on a core agent and deterministically prove it won't break invariants, you get something new: a provably correct agent. What exactly can this scenario bring? He gave a very concrete picture: suppose you submit a claim today and have to wait a month to get the result. If an insurance company could confidently run this fully automatically, the results could be out in 10 seconds. The reason this can't be done now is that the process requires human intervention. He was very conservative about the timeline, saying there will be preliminary results next year, followed by continuous iteration.

He calls this one of the next big bets, which is adding a deterministic side to non-deterministic models without sacrificing their advantages. He added a vivid analogy: "If you can set a rule telling the agent to never attempt a privilege escalation, then even if a magic button to do so is placed in front of it, it won't touch it." Regarding open source versus closed source, Garman didn't pretend to know everything; he admitted he wasn't sure if most inference would run on open-weight models in the future, but he observed a trend of frontier labs working harder to lock down models, making distillation more difficult. If these lockdowns are. successful, the progress of open-weight models might slow down. Regarding the situation in China, he didn't beat around the bush either. He believes that almost all successful open-weight models today succeed because they can distill from frontier models. If this path is blocked—for instance, by hiding inference processes, controlling tokens , or encrypting outputs—the pace of open-source models could be affected. But he also said it might not be, because someone will always start from first principles, and he himself is a model builder. Another variable is cost ; frontier model companies have discovered that distilling their own models works better than anything else,. so they can create smaller, cheaper versions internally and sell them at a lower price. Over the past few months, both OpenAI and Anthropic have done this . So, Jassy's assessment is that these companies won't easily give up 90%of their market share. They have already invested huge fixed costs and have enough incentive to build small models themselves to lower prices; this will be an interesting game to watch. As for AWS's position, he put it clearly: he supports whoever makes it work. As long as everything runs on Bedrock, customers can use the best. In the latter part of the conversation, we discussed AWS's position within Amazon. One figure. perfectly illustrates this: AWS contributes about 23%of Amazon's revenue but accounts for roughly 63%of its operating profit. Jassy has been at Amazon for 20 years. In his view, this place encourages you to create and encourages you to think big enough. Twenty years ago, no one would have imagined that an online bookstore would become a top global tech giant, providing underlying computing power to governments and banks worldwide. When they first pitched the idea of the " cloud" to Jeff Bezos back then, his reaction was, "That’s fantastic!" My own assessment is that Amazon is now the largest database company in the world. This wasn't something planned out either . They picked a very smart team and had. them build a brand-new cloud database, which eventually became Aurora. There is another advantage that outsiders might not notice: Amazon itself is one of AWS's largest customers, as well as one of the world's largest and most complex retail applications. It has been built on top of AWS since day one. This customer submits requirements earlier and more aggressively than any external client. Can this demand be met today? Can that cluster be expanded tomorrow? This pressure, in turn, is what actually refined and polished the product. Discussing it to this point, the outline of the whole situation is actually quite clear. The revenue goal is not just a slogan; it rests on three things. The.

explosion of inference hasn't started yet, and the supply of computing power will be tight for a few years. What truly determines the ceiling is whether companies can be assured enough to hand over their core businesses and agents. Of these three, the first two are issues of money and power, while the third is an issue of trust. And trust is much harder to build than a data center. What do you think? When agents can truly choose, write, integrate, and finish tasks on their own, how much authority would you be willing to hand over? Would you hand it over to a system that can be clearly calculated, or to one that is smarter but cannot be clearly explained ? This choice may determine who pulls. ahead in the coming years more than computing power itself. Thanks for watching, and see you next time.

作者指出，知名科技訪談者 Dwarkesh Patel 原本認為超級人工智慧尚需至少十年以上才會現身，但在短短幾個月內其觀點發生了激進的轉變，如今認為 AI 極可能在短短數年甚至數月內，便在研究領域達到人類頂級專家的水準。改變這項判斷的首要依據是AI 內部研發速度的翻倍。根據評估，部分前沿實驗室在明確任務上的進展已達一年前的兩倍；OpenAI 前 10% 的研究員調用內部代理（Agent）的支出暴增數倍，而 DeepMind 更有超過四分之一的研究工作直接由 AI 主導，顯示 AI 研發自我加速的齒輪已經開始轉動。

解題能力的飛躍與機器學習研究的本質

作者進一步探討第二個核心依據：數學與明確問題的求解能力。AI 在短短數年間從無法正確計算四位數加法，迅速躍升至奧數金牌水準，甚至在 88 小時內解決了千禧年大獎問題。作者指出，機器學習研究與純數學不同，它不仰賴深奧優雅的新理論，而是著重於能實際訓練出更強模型的「實用配方」。以奠定當代大模型基礎的 Transformer 架構為例，其各項核心組件早就存在，真正欠缺的是大量微調實驗與極佳的研究品味。具備強大驗證與組合能力的 AI 恰好最擅長此道，因此作者推論，自動化研究員在 2028 年甚至最快在 2027 年追平人類頂尖專家，將是極可能發生的現實。

作者分析，一旦 AI 研究能力比肩頂尖人類，進展將因速度更快、智商更高、規模更大三大維度而全面提速。AI 無需休息且運算迅捷，單兵產出約為人類的 50 倍；同時，它能將每一位「研究員」的水準拉升至頂尖專家層級，並以成千上萬個代理並行推進模組化任務。最後，作者點出未來技術走向的核心拉鋸：遞歸自我提升（RSI）與「好想法愈來愈難找」之間的競速。一旦 AI 自我迭代變聰明的速度徹底壓過難題遞增的阻力，世界便可能迎來短短數月內逼近晶片物理極限的純軟體起飛，徹底重塑人類文明的科技邊界。

open-ended. AI will have to learn to navigate an unimaginably large number of virtual worlds; compared to today’s video games, these would be like a Bugatti compared to a horse-drawn carriage. They did need experience, but it took years, not decades. Whatever happened in their minds, AI should be able to replicate or even surpass it; there is no reason to. believe humans have reached the ceiling for how fast one can learn from experience. Moreover, AI has another advantage: it can accumulate years of deployment experience in just a few calendar days. If you want a future AI to manage a Fortune 500 company better than the current CEO, how long would it take to get up to speed? On the first morning, have it shadow the CEO, and it could read every email, every instant message, and every document in the company's history. By the end of the first day, its multiple avatars could have interviewed every employee and major client. It indeed cannot access feedback that requires months of waiting.

, such as next quarter's financial results, but even with this limitation, he still expects such AI to reach top-tier human levels in all fields within months of its development. According to his median scenario, that is something that will happen in 2028 or 2029. Over the past five years, even without any AI assistance, global AI computing power has roughly tripled every year. AI created by sparks will be particularly adept at helping us continue to scale up. compute—for example, by designing new AI chips, planning new power plants, or even remotely controlling robots to build facilities and data centers. The only difference is that this path takes years to reach the same destination that purely hardware-based approaches could reach in just a few months. This superintelligence, which relates to humans as we relate to chimpanzees—for this video, I’ve included a technical argument at the end to explain why AI research is, in principle, verifiable. This part is a bit hard-core, so I’ll summarize the key points for you. AI R& D is roughly divided into three main areas: pre-training, post-training, and inference efficiency, each with concrete metrics that can serve directly as. training objectives. These three areas combined perfectly cover the entirety of algorithmic progress. So, it’s not surprising that overall AI progress can be used as a training objective; since AI training happens inside data centers , the things we do to improve models are exactly what data centers can measure. First, let’s look at pre-training: you can set a target for a model to reach a fixed loss on a small-scale model using as little compute as possible. Loss on a test set is a measurable value, very easy to verify, and even rankable. You can design an environment to see if the model can predict whether algorithmic. improvements that work at one parameter scale will still hold true at a scale of 10 billion parameters. Post-training also has proxy metrics, such as dropping a model into an environment it has never seen to see how quickly it adapts to achieve good results; ByteDance’s AdaBench benchmark measures exactly this type of capability. Inside ByteDance, there is also a benchmark called "C," which contains about 500 real-world problems that their researchers and engineers have solved this year. Every benchmark is also a reinforcement learning environment, which essentially tasks the model with replicating the frontier progress humans have made in the last three to six months; inference. efficiency is even easier to measure, as GPU usage, KV cache size per token, and latency are all readily available numbers. Tucked inside this is a counterintuitive piece of information: the lab Magic recently announced that they used about half the compute of the original GPT-3 to train a foundational model capable of rivaling leading open-weights models like DeepSeek-V 4 Pro. At today’s prices, that amount of compute is worth approximately $ 500,000 . So he concludes that pre-training hasn't hit a ceiling; increasing it by several orders of magnitude is entirely possible. recursive self-improvement. First point : continual learning. For the past year and a half, he has maintained that the core capability AI lacks today is learning from work experience. Every new session is like its first day on the job ; a session can only retain a few hours of information, failing to accumulate the feedback and know-how that takes weeks or months to build. In December 2025, he was still saying it was incredible that these systems, lacking even the basic learning abilities of a child, were trying to crack the AGI algorithms that have baffled humanity for over half a century. But now he's changed his tune, for two reasons. First , solving continual learning might not. require a major architectural breakthrough; scaling up in-context learning to make sessions effectively last longer, allowing a single instance to learn while it works, might be enough . Second, continual learning is itself a research problem with clear validation metrics, similar to solving a math problem. If you had asked him two years ago to compare the Navier-Stokes equations with continual learning, asking which is harder to solve, he wouldn't have thought the answer was obviously the former. His analogy is clever: current models lack long-term memory, like the clumsiest interns, yet they are already solving millennial-old problems. It's like someone moving down the track while doing cartwheels, yet. still keeping pace with Usain Bolt. Who says that doing cartwheels means they can't win the race? However, he still leaves room for doubt; if we fail to solve continual learning in the next few years, and models can't compensate with other advantages, that remains a serious possibility. That is why he gave a 25% probability that automating top-tier research at the level of Ilya Sutskever won't happen until after 2032. Second point: data. Data is the primary input for AI progress. If data doesn't keep up , how can recursive self-improvement occur? His answer is that the entity compiling the data is the AI itself. He conducted research with Princeton. student Jerry Han, finding that over the past six years of pre-training progress , gains from data improvements outweighed gains from model improvements by more than three times. And so-called data improvement is essentially figuring out which methods can filter existing data and generate new synthetic data to lower the loss function, which is very similar to regular AI research work. A paper published on post-training new models confirms this; they found that systematic improvements in the scale, diversity, and verifiability of synthetic data environments basically account for all observed gains. And the way these environments are constructed. is itself becoming increasingly automated. Third, experimental compute. While mathematics can produce new discoveries with just a pen and paper, AI research requires running actual experiments, burning both compute and time. As the number of researchers grows , won't the experimental compute allocated to each person become diluted ? He did the math: if labs increase their compute by more than four times each year, following this trend, by the end of 2027, OpenAI could provide 10,000 agents—the same number of agents involved in solving that millennial prize problem. Every agent would be able to be allocated enough compute to run a GPT-3 scale training session every single day. The final model in the.

original 2017 Transformer paper only used 8 P100s for three days; that amount of compute costs about 50 dollars today , which is only one ten-thousandth of the compute used to train GPT-3. If researchers like Ilya and X2 had the experimental compute to train a GPT-3 scale model every day, they might be a bit slower than they are now. But if they just sat there and couldn't produce any meaningful progress, only complaining that the cluster was too small, he would be very surprised. Moreover, the reason labs use compute the way they do today is because researchers 'time is far scarcer than compute; the annual compensation for top researchers can reach hundreds of. millions of dollars. The way we use it today doesn't show how efficient it could be once compute becomes the main bottleneck. Agent swarms have two advantages humans can't match: first, trading labor for compute—reading every training trajectory, and as soon as a task breaks, immediately stopping to rebuild the entire environment. Small-scale experiments can be run relentlessly. Before pooling compute for a large experiment, we should spend subjective decades designing the most information-dense joint experiments, then spend another subjective few decades analyzing the results to invent better scientific methods, extracting every bit of information from small experiments. The GPT-4 paper stated that they could predict the loss of the final. model using a model with 10,000 times less compute. Scaling phenomena like this allow researchers to predict optimal hyperparameters for large training runs from models 100 times smaller. He remembers a conversation with a researcher who once said: the gods above must surely follow the same principles as the ants below. After hearing the whole argument, you’ll find his position is actually more restrained than the title suggests. The median year is set to 2028, with room left for 2027 and after 2032, splitting the probability of software-only and "spark " at 50%each. What he really wants to say is that recursive self-improvement. might have already started. So, do you think his judgment is correct? Feel free to leave a comment below. Thanks for watching, and we’ll see you in the next one.

An independent evaluator spent three months embedded at METAMIND, concluding that this lab’s AI progress on well-defined tasks is already twice as fast as it was a year ago. And a large part of this acceleration likely comes from their. extensive use of AI for R&D. OpenAI disclosed internal data in September this year showing that the top 10%of researchers using AI increased their daily spending on internal agents from about $ 1,000 at the start of the year to over $ 7,000 by the end of August. DeepMind also stated in September that AI now leads 26%of their research work, a figure that was under 1%back in February. With internal R&D speeds doubled, this is the first basis for his change in judgment. The second basis is mathematics; in his words, today’s AI. solves well-defined math problems like a hot knife through butter. The progress bar looks like this: 2023 models couldn't even get four-digit addition right, 2024 saw near-total failure in high school math competitions, 2025 brought International Math Olympiad gold , and earlier this year, they began tackling niche unsolved problems. And just one month before he released his video, AI solved a Millennium Prize problem in 88 hours. He quoted a line from the novel*East of Eden*: "One thing is certain about the fall of gods: they do not just fall a little; they crash to. the ground and shatter into pieces." Of course, some people are pouring cold water on this. T. B. O'Dea recently wrote: "While AI systems are starting to automate mathematical proofs, there is currently little evidence that they can pose fruitful questions or open up profound new fields of mathematics."" That statement is correct, but Delip Rao turns it around: 'A system that cannot yet ask profound questions has already solved a millennium prize problem.'"" Moreover, he argues that this ability to solve well-defined problems is even more critical for machine learning research than for pure mathematics.""The core of mathematical research is to expand human.

understanding of concepts, proposing new frameworks like topology or group theory , which is more fundamental than solving problems. But in AI research, the priorities are reversed; experimentalists only care if a new recipe can practically train a model to be smarter, not whether the theory is elegant.""The progress of deep learning over the past 15 years hasn't really relied on new theories.""He gives a very specific example: the Transformer."" This architecture, which defines the entire era of large language models, had all its core components known before the 2017 paper was published. Researchers active at the time were well aware that attention mechanisms could improve. parallel training and allow information to pass through longer sequences."" Chris Olah was in that circle back then ; he feels the Transformer simply combined existing, effective ideas in a rather radical and natural way.""So why wasn't it invented sooner?""Because this architecture required five or six additional tweaks before it could significantly outperform the best solutions of that time.""Almost all the parts had been sitting in the literature for years, but no one knew exactly how to put them together. This requires excellent research taste and a massive number of small experiments; consistently and smartly testing dozens. of combinations is precisely the strength AI has shown in mathematics."" His conclusion is straightforward: since AlexNet sparked the deep learning revolution in 2012, the biggest breakthrough in machine learning has been the Transformer. And something like this could be invented by a model at the level of Claude 3, provided Chris Olah asked it to work extremely hard on improving the attention mechanism.""Of course, some aspects of AI research are harder to verify than math. Otherwise, if we clearly have models capable of autonomously solving millennium problems , why haven't we fired all the researchers yet?""His judgment is that the verifiability of AI research is. already high enough.""If he had to choose a median year for automated researchers to reach the level of top human experts, he would choose 2028, assuming labs keep moving at full speed , don't proactively slow down, and aren't suppressed by the government. Why could it be done within a few years?"" The reason he gives is that in every field where answers can be verified and AI can practice for thousands of rounds , AI has gone from being worse than most people to surpassing the very best in just a few short years." It’s the same for programming competitions and solving clear-cut math problems; the model’s generalization ability goes far beyond its direct training. OpenAI's model wasn't built by grinding through other. millennium prize problems; it was trained on vast amounts of easier math and then directly transferred to unsolved ones. He also acknowledges the flip side: some crucial aspects are indeed difficult to automate. It’s hard to predict this in advance, but he estimates there is at least a 25%chance that this won't be achieved until after 2030. But conversely, it could be much faster. Some well-informed researchers he knows, who have had great track records in the past few years, believe AI could surpass top-tier humans in AI research as early as next year. Taking the conclusion that progress has doubled and plugging it directly into "takeoff"

models also points to around 2027. Ajeya Cotra, who has been on his show, once said that if we accept the claim that AI is nearly doubling its own rate of progress, and assume this acceleration happens smoothly. Then the most direct inference is that we will reach extreme superintelligence within a year. He hasn't set 2027 as the median simply because he’s not quite confident in such straightforward models, but in his own words, we shouldn't be surprised if we hit this milestone next year; we should be prepared. Once AI’s research capabilities match the very best humans , why would progress accelerate so. drastically? He gave three reasons: faster, smarter, and more. First, speed : today’s AI works about ten times faster than humans, and automated researchers don't need to sleep, working nights and weekends. Altogether, each automated researcher’s weekly output is about 50 times that of a human. Of course, that doesn't mean AI progress will immediately accelerate 50-fold; experimental compute is still a bottleneck, so experiments won't run faster, leading to diminishing returns. But even with steep diminishing returns , algorithmic progress will still be several times faster. Next, smarter: his sense is that at a frontier lab, about. 80%of algorithmic progress comes from the top 50 researchers. It’s no wonder Mark Zuckerberg is willing to spend hundreds of millions of dollars to recruit the best talent. In an automated company, where every researcher and engineer reaches the level of today’s top humans, that in itself is another significant acceleration. Finally, quantity: the "human sea" tactic isn't a cure-all; for instance, having a group of agents write a novel isn't necessarily much faster than one agent. But some tasks are inherently suited for parallelism. His video features an animation of a group of agents collaborating to turn Fermat's Last Theorem into a formal proof. The project. has thousands of modular subtasks that can be advanced independently, with each agent able to verify its own work on the spot. AI research is more like proving theorems than writing novels; it has plenty of independent modular work and verifiable progress metrics, where 1,000 methods can be tested simultaneously to see which is best, and this can be done at every stage of the process. He doesn't shy away from the fact that there are diminishing returns here— 100,000 collaborators don't mean a 100,000 x speedup; it probably wouldn't even be 100x. However, given the nature of AI research, he also finds it implausible that increasing labor by several orders of magnitude wouldn't even result in a several-fold speedup. Next is the most interesting part of the entire argument: will this speed be maintained, continue to accelerate, or slow down? He says this question is even more important than how fast the initial speed is. There are two opposing forces here: one is Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI), where automated researchers will keep getting faster, smarter, and more numerous. The other force is that good ideas are becoming increasingly hard to find. Note that this is already happening: AI companies have to quadruple their annual R&D compute and double their headcount just to maintain the same rate of progress. If the speed at which AI gets smarter outpaces the.

speed at which ideas get harder to find , we will see what is called a "pure software takeoff." In this scenario, even without adding any more compute, the AI collective will rapidly iterate into increasingly smarter versions of itself. They would become superintelligences that push against the physical limits of current chips within a few short months. Conversely, if ideas get harder to find faster, the result is what he calls a "Sparks" scenario: one calendar year yields progress that would take three to six years at current speeds, and then everything slows down until we build more compute. This is because even these super-genius-level automated researchers need to run. larger-scale experiments to continue making breakthroughs. He estimates the probability of these two scenarios at roughly half and half—50%for "Sparks" and 50%for "pure software takeoff." It’s a passable coder that can complete a simple Python function, but is otherwise basically a useless toy ; whereas SOTA models can build complete video games from scratch and produce so. many mathematical contributions that we’ve become numb to it. In the past four years, we have gone from a preschooler to a genius student. If we span a similarly large interval starting from 2027 or 2028, we will likely achieve an intelligence that far surpasses humans in any field that is even slightly verifiable. Designing the next generation of AI accelerators, it will outperform NVIDIA; given equal market access, it will be more profitable than any human-run startup or firm today. Give it remote control over a materials science lab to find room-temperature superconductors, and it will be better at it than the rest of. humanity combined. You might ask, how could a superintelligence trained in a data center possibly defeat human experts in fields that require years of real-world experience? After all, our current way of making AI smarter relies on tasks that can be automatically graded in data centers, such as writing code to pass unit tests or solving open-ended math problems. How do you train an AI to start a business, win a lawsuit, execute a profitable daily trade, or help a candidate win an election? The processes for these tasks require interaction with the real world and cannot be replicated in a server room. His answer is not to expect to. bake the answers to every real-world problem directly into the model, but rather to focus on the ability to quickly master new situations, even in these hard-to-verify fields. Accomplishing tasks requires two things : domain knowledge and a set of more general skills—the kind that capable people share, such as finding relevant information, planning, pushing forward through errors and obstacles, documenting what is learned, and collaborating with others. During recursive self-improvement, automation engineers will build reinforcement learning environments that are tens of thousands of times more complex than today’s—larger in scale, longer in duration, higher in quality, and more.

open-ended. AI will have to learn to navigate an unimaginably large number of virtual worlds; compared to today’s video games, these would be like a Bugatti compared to a horse-drawn carriage. They will be harder, messier, larger, and closer to reality than anything built for human entertainment, and they will require AI to cooperate or compete with other AI teams over long periods. For instance, throw an AI into a simulated economy with millions of other AIs and task it with co-founding a successful company. It won't just dwell on idealized company structures; instead , it will undergo the equivalent of centuries of corporate competition to. figure out the best ways to organize. You can use history for backtesting: train it only on data up to 1700 to see if it can derive general relativity, or give it only newspapers up to 1962 to see if it can predict how the Cuban Missile Crisis unfolds. Why should we believe that this training will transfer into general-purpose competence? He provided a very bold analogy about human evolution. Our general cognitive architecture was shaped by evolution, and evolution is a very crude optimization process that simply passes on a set of standard genes. In the ancestral environment, the task of this. standard was hunting, avoiding predators , and maintaining tribal status; these are only a tiny fraction of the tasks humans can handle today. Evolution never specifically optimized us to write code , design advanced semiconductors, lead nations of millions, or pioneer new branches of mathematics; yet, in the process of optimizing for survival on the savanna, it inadvertently created a general-purpose learner. If evolution could accomplish that, AI companies, with clear goals and deliberate training , can certainly go even further. Of course, even smarter learners cannot figure everything out just by staying in. a data center. To surpass the top human experts, they still need a bit of real-world experience. Napoleon was 27 when he had already defeated much larger armies of European powers, and Rockefeller had only been in the oil industry for two years before running one of the world's largest refineries. They did need experience, but it took years, not decades. Whatever happened in their minds, AI should be able to replicate or even surpass it; there is no reason to. believe humans have reached the ceiling for how fast one can learn from experience. Moreover, AI has another advantage: it can accumulate years of deployment experience in just a few calendar days. If you want a future AI to manage a Fortune 500 company better than the current CEO, how long would it take to get up to speed? On the first morning, have it shadow the CEO, and it could read every email, every instant message, and every document in the company's history. By the end of the first day, its multiple avatars could have interviewed every employee and major client. It indeed cannot access feedback that requires months of waiting.

, such as next quarter's financial results, but even with this limitation, he still expects such AI to reach top-tier human levels in all fields within months of its development. According to his median scenario, that is something that will happen in 2028 or 2029. And the story doesn't end there; even if progress at the software level gradually plateaus, AI will continue to improve by increasing computing power. Over the past five years, even without any AI assistance, global AI computing power has roughly tripled every year. AI created by sparks will be particularly adept at helping us continue to scale up. compute—for example, by designing new AI chips, planning new power plants, or even remotely controlling robots to build facilities and data centers. The only difference is that this path takes years to reach the same destination that purely hardware-based approaches could reach in just a few months. This superintelligence, which relates to humans as we relate to chimpanzees—for this video, I’ve included a technical argument at the end to explain why AI research is, in principle, verifiable. This part is a bit hard-core, so I’ll summarize the key points for you. AI R& D is roughly divided into three main areas: pre-training, post-training, and inference efficiency, each with concrete metrics that can serve directly as. training objectives. These three areas combined perfectly cover the entirety of algorithmic progress. So, it’s not surprising that overall AI progress can be used as a training objective; since AI training happens inside data centers , the things we do to improve models are exactly what data centers can measure. First, let’s look at pre-training: you can set a target for a model to reach a fixed loss on a small-scale model using as little compute as possible. Loss on a test set is a measurable value, very easy to verify, and even rankable. You can design an environment to see if the model can predict whether algorithmic. improvements that work at one parameter scale will still hold true at a scale of 10 billion parameters. Post-training also has proxy metrics, such as dropping a model into an environment it has never seen to see how quickly it adapts to achieve good results; ByteDance’s AdaBench benchmark measures exactly this type of capability. Inside ByteDance, there is also a benchmark called "C," which contains about 500 real-world problems that their researchers and engineers have solved this year. Every benchmark is also a reinforcement learning environment, which essentially tasks the model with replicating the frontier progress humans have made in the last three to six months; inference. efficiency is even easier to measure, as GPU usage, KV cache size per token, and latency are all readily available numbers. Finally, let's see how he addresses the harshest criticism, namely the three strongest arguments against.

recursive self-improvement. First point : continual learning. For the past year and a half, he has maintained that the core capability AI lacks today is learning from work experience. Every new session is like its first day on the job ; a session can only retain a few hours of information, failing to accumulate the feedback and know-how that takes weeks or months to build. In December 2025, he was still saying it was incredible that these systems, lacking even the basic learning abilities of a child, were trying to crack the AGI algorithms that have baffled humanity for over half a century. If you had asked him two years ago to compare the Navier-Stokes equations with continual learning, asking which is harder to solve, he wouldn't have thought the answer was obviously the former. 摘要

破除 AI 經濟神話：理性看待成長與失業衝擊

作者大飛指出，圍繞當前 AI 熱潮的兩大極端預測——10% 的經濟成長率以及短期內失業率暴增三倍——在 OpenAI 首位首席經濟學家 Ronnie Chatterji 眼中均不切實際。Chatterji 認為，美國經濟只要增加 1% 至 2% 的成長率就已是翻天覆地的變革，而失業率哪怕僅微幅上升 0.5 到 1 個百分點，便足以引發嚴重的社會動盪；將 2020 年因疫情全面封城的極端經驗套用於未來 12 到 18 個月的 AI 衝擊，本質上是基準校準的錯誤。

從晶片法案到 OpenAI：首席經濟學家的職責與布局

曾深度參與美國《晶片法案》（CHIPS Act）推動的 Chatterji，在與 OpenAI 探討半導體議題的過程中，親手撰寫了首席經濟學家的職務描述，最終因緣際會親自接下該重任。他打造了一支融合經濟學博士、數據科學家與具備跨部門推進力的MBA 專案經理團隊。頂尖 AI 實驗室引進經濟學家的目的，除了將龐大的用戶數據解讀給商務部或各國央行等決策機構外，更關鍵的是研究未來工作者管理AI Agent（代理人）時，所催生出的全新組織行為與激勵機制。

未來 12 至 18 個月的趨勢：深層系統串接與職能界線模糊

展望未來一年半的局勢，Chatterji 提出三大核心觀察：第一，AI 革命才剛要深度滲透企業，關鍵在於跨出問答機器人形式，將連接器（Connectors）深度整合至現有企業系統中；第二，就業市場不會直接面臨全面淘汰，而是工作實質內容的轉變，許多員工已開始跨出既有職務描述，例如財務人員執行行銷任務、公關人員自主跑數據；第三，龐大的硬體資本支出已率先推動 GDP 數字，但實質的生產力躍升將在未來一年多內陸續浮現於統計數據中。

法務與人資的逆勢突圍與全球 AI 版圖的分歧

在企業內部落地節奏上，Chatterji 觀察到法務與人資部門因具備密集的流程與豐富的結構化數據，轉型速度出乎意料地名列前茅；以 OpenAI 內部為例，非技術部門全面深度整合 AI 僅比技術團隊落後約四至五個月。放大至全球格局，日本與南韓依託強大的晶片供應鏈與人口結構挑戰積極擁抱 AI；印尼與巴西則受惠於 18 至 25 歲的年輕人口紅利，展現超乎預期的活躍度；歐洲則深陷於科技自主架構與監管平衡的激烈辯論。為真實評測勞動力替代情況，OpenAI 亦推出依據美國勞工部 O*NET 架構的 JDBench 基準測試，藉由 44 種真實職業情境精準檢驗模型的實務能力。
