He wants people with PhDs and data science backgrounds, but also people who are capable of driving things forward within the organization. Having worked in government, I know how hard it is to push things across departments, so I specifically recruited people with MBA backgrounds who have actually managed projects. In the end, this team was formed by a mix of project managers, data scientists, and economists. Tech companies hiring economists began roughly at the start of this century. When Hal Varian was still teaching at Berkeley, Chatterjee was his student and used his textbooks. Later, when Varian joined Google, the academic world was. shaken; back then, academics joining corporations was extremely rare. Later on, more and more economists entered tech firms. So why does a frontier lab need someone like this? The first reason is data. Beyond a handful of global institutions, we possess some of the richest data on AI usage in the consumer sector. This data needs to be interpreted and presented to institutions like the Department of Commerce or the Bank of England to help them understand what is happening in the industry. Although the company has a top-tier data science team, data scientists usually focus on product decisions; we need someone to step out.

of the lab and look at the broader socioeconomic structure. The second reason is even more novel: the company is creating a new class of economic participants. His hypothesis is that the next generation of workers will likely manage more AI agents than human colleagues. What exactly are the behavioral patterns of these agents? What kind of organizational structures will they spawn, and what incentive mechanisms should be used to regulate them? Economists have a ready-made toolkit for these questions. Looking at the next 12 to 18 months, he predicts three things will happen, and they are already emerging. First, the revolution will truly penetrate enterprises. He. says we are still at a very early stage . This might sound strange to say in San Francisco, but in the rest of the world , it is indeed just getting started. If we look at companies using AI now, the proportion that have truly enabled connectors to integrate AI into existing software is still very small. Yet this step is crucial; if AI doesn't have access to your computers and systems and is just a Q&A bot, its value clearly cannot be realized. Second, the job market won't change as drastically as many expect; what will change is the work content beneath the surface. He offered an observation: a large portion of work has already moved beyond job descriptions—for instance, finance. people are now handling marketing tasks , and corporate communications staff can run their own data. People are stepping outside their job boundaries to do things they’ve never done before. As more people in companies gain access to agents, this trend will only accelerate . Regarding productivity statistics, he said that AI has already entered GDP through capital expenditure, with hardware investment on a massive scale. However, economists are really eyeing productivity, and he expects more significant changes in this area over the next 12 to 18 months. As for the discussion about those two inflated numbers, they are essentially the same issue regarding our calibration of scale. . Moving on, the host asked a question that is easily overlooked: which department will actually make the first move? Chatterjee’s answer was somewhat counterintuitive. He said that legal and human resources—two departments many feel are far removed from AI—should not be underestimated. Within OpenAI, he observed the legal department transforming its workflow with AI as quickly as any team he has ever seen. He added a caveat that the legal profession itself is a biased sample and cannot fully represent the outside world. Regarding the pace of internal corporate adoption, using OpenAI as an example: in November 2025, various groups in San Francisco were having heated discussions. , with people sharing amazing use cases , but it wasn't until April and May 2026 that non-research and non-engineering departments became as deeply integrated with AI as the technical teams. He himself didn't fully start utilizing it until that time. According to him, as an economist with so many degrees who does data analysis every day, he is still classified as "non-technical" in the company system. Therefore, there is roughly a four to five-month lag between technical and non-technical departments . He emphasized that not every company is like OpenAI, but functions like legal and HR, which are process-intensive with abundant structured data, are what he. will be focusing on. The gap between enterprises is also widening. Some companies have already tapped into the potential of their internal super-users , while the so-called median adopters are still a long way from that step. This gap is not only widening, but it will also directly impact how much AI can be converted into economic results. When scaled to the national level, the divergence is even greater. Japan and South Korea are optimistic about AI's ability to transform the economy, driven by their past technological successes, demographics different from the West, and a group of companies that have already tasted the benefits. Looking at South Korea’s chip supply chain, with SK Hynix and Samsung leading the way, the effects are clearly visible. Enterprises.

in these regions are heavy users of AI, and because they were already connected to other technologies, the adoption of generative AI has been very smooth. A positive surprise is Indonesia and Brazil, where usage rates are much higher than he expected. Ou will release the relevant data, attributing a large part of the reason to a young population . People aged 18 to 25 are high-frequency AI users, a pattern seen globally. In Jakarta universities, he saw students discussing AI at a level almost identical to San Francisco, with no sense of lag. India is no longer a surprise; he attended an AI conference and was still deeply struck by the number of companies emerging around AI. More interesting are the large corporate groups. Having studied business school cases, they don't want to be the dinosaurs that get disrupted and are working hard to ensure they use AI. At the other end is Europe, where the struggle is two-fold: how to generate productivity from AI in enterprises, and how to safeguard core segments of their key tech stack amid globalization's retreat and shifting geopolitics. Since the Draghi memorandum was released, the internal debate in Europe has been intense. Chatterjee is reluctant to call it negative; he prefers to describe it as a genuine debate about what role AI should play in business and society. At. this point, the conversation shifted to a topic directly related to whether AI will take away jobs. OpenAI has created a benchmark test called JDBench. It doesn't use test questions, but instead uses real-world work to challenge the models. This is a test where experienced practitioners from 44 professions create questions and grade the models on whether they can do the job. The logic starts with a task list; the U.S. Department of Labor has a system called O*NET that breaks every profession down into individual tasks. With this list, one can ask: "Can AI do this task better than a human?" That is where the problem lies. Many people initially assume that. if a job has ten tasks and AI can do five of them better, then that person has a 50%chance of losing their job. But Chatterjee says that is not how things work at all. Chatterjee gave an example involving his own father. In 1984, his father installed a computer in his office. His father was an economics professor who needed to run large regressions. Before the computer, he had to carry stacks of punch cards into the machine room. Once broken down by task, the computer could do almost every part of the professor's job, but he didn't lose his job in 1984. He used the computer to run bigger regressions, build more models, and write more papers. . This example illustrates one thing: work being covered by AI does not mean being replaced by AI. Sometimes, it is quite the opposite; being covered means you have the opportunity to leverage it . Another reason less often mentioned is that tasks are endogenous; no one tells you to just do these ten things, as you have a higher goal, and tasks emerge to serve that objective. Satya's perspective on entrepreneurship is also related to his academic background. His doctoral dissertation studied entrepreneurship, which was not a mainstream topic at the time. Years later, seeing AI become another accelerator for startups and company. formation, he values the lessons of failure most; when he first started studying entrepreneurship, he thought the outcome was binary—either you build a company, or you end up with nothing. Later, after talking to those who had actually walked that path, he discovered that failure is often where one learns the most, and it can also be the prelude to the next great company. There are also some people who, only after starting a business, realize they are better suited as co-founders or simply working for someone else. Therefore, the faster the process, the better; one of the biggest benefits of AI is that it helps people reach that conclusion more quickly. This means there will be more failures, but fortunately, there will also be more successes, and the path for.

solo-entrepreneurship has been opened up . In many places, finding a co-founder is difficult, and hiring a Chief Marketing Officer is even harder; now these people can get started faster, leveraging an AI expert to gain knowledge that was previously out of reach. He feels this is a very tangible form of empowerment. Is this reflected in the data? The answer is yes. About half a year ago, a report was released showing that roughly 4 million Americans had used ChatGPT in some phase of starting a business. The aspect he values the most is brainstorming. He wrote a paper long ago on the startup process, which mentioned an incredible conclusion: the most common cause of. failure is actually the step of sharing the idea with others and getting feedback. Many people get stuck there, but now you can bypass that and directly ask AI for its take on the idea to get constructive feedback. Small businesses already in operation also benefit; restaurants can figure out which dishes should be on the menu, which sell well, and whether their selections are correct . These tasks used to require hiring expensive consultants, but now AI can provide a reasonably accurate answer. Returning to the macro level, has AI really entered the productivity data? His answer is divided into two parts. The first half is that AI is already reflected in GDP, and we must honestly. admit that. Looking at capital expenditure, 40 basis points to one percentage point of U.S. GDP growth can be attributed to AI infrastructure investment. It is not a small amount; it is a solid, genuine boost. And the second half of his point is that the next step is to convert this into productivity, or what economists call total factor productivity. He has seen that the data cited by Feynman aligns with the early emergence of AI effects, but it cannot be fully confirmed yet that AI is the cause; such verification often only happens in hindsight. He cited the famous 1995 Fed meeting where Alan Greenspan was convinced he saw productivity gains from technology,. while Janet Yellen said she hadn't seen it in the data yet. The final result was that the data was significantly revised upward later, so he judges that we might be at the beginning of that same moment , but it will take time before he can point to the data and say this is AI. He is confident in the market and in AI; business leaders are doubling down on investments and promoting them organization-wide, so they must be seeing returns, which will eventually translate into productivity. It just won't happen at all companies simultaneously, nor will it occur synchronously in every corner of the globe. He used that quote from William Gibson to summarize his answer: "The. future is already here—it's just not evenly distributed." As a joke, Gibson himself told friends he never actually said that, but he is quite happy to own it. So, if capital expenditure drives up demand and inflation, while productivity pulls inflation down, how will this tug-of-war play out? He says economists love this kind of game; inflation has many causes, and among the factors pushing it up today are the global situation, food prices, and a bunch of variables related to AI. The part related to AI depends on the hardware supply chain; for example, the price of DRAM memory has risen very sharply over. the past year. He believes that inflation caused by supply chain bottlenecks only accounts for a small piece, and as infrastructure expands and supply catches up, this part will gradually recede, which of course also depends on competition among companies in the chain. In the long run, it suppresses the force AI has to lower prices; it might not be visible within two years, but if we take a longer view , this deflationary effect will be significant. Some call this the "Jevons Paradox," but he prefers to call it a downward-sloping demand curve: if you lower the cost of completing a task, as long as there is enough elasticity, demand will rise, and many markets will expand as a result; he has already seen.

signs of this in his own research. If AI continues to deliver, what would it look like if we jumped straight to 2031? His approach is to look at countries first; the nations leading in adoption rates will reap the most dividends, and the United States is one of them. History will repeat itself, perhaps on an even larger scale. Stanford's Nick Bloom, John Van Reenen, and Raffaella Sadun famously analyzed IT adoption in US and UK firms. US firms had higher adoption rates and better management practices, leading to higher productivity—a dividend that boosted the US economy for. years. If the returns on AI are as expected, we will see a similar trajectory: US firms will fully embrace AI and use that capability globally to lift economic growth. An increase of one to two percentage points, or even three to four, would be a massive change. Looking at the employment structure, he predicts massive growth in education and healthcare. The logic is simple: the wealthier a society, the more it spends on education and healthcare. Once the AI dividend arrives, truly important priorities will emerge, with caring for people and educating the next generation at the forefront. Furthermore, history shows that when technology enters these. two fields, it often simultaneously creates a demand for more human labor. However, there is also a preference issue. He says if he had to choose between replacing a kindergarten teacher with a robot or shrinking class sizes so two teachers could instruct half the number of students, he would choose the latter. He believes most Americans feel the same regarding doctors, nurses, and caregivers. The real suspense lies in wages. Education and healthcare account for about one-seventh of US jobs. If we shift the economic focus to these areas but the new positions pay less than previous jobs, there is no gain—so. compensation for these roles must rise. The entertainment industry is another possible engine; he jokes about how many children now say they want to be influencers when they grow up. Economists love to track new job titles . It used to be cybersecurity experts; now it might be influencers. Even the term "podcaster" hasn't been around for very many years. Using AI and other tools to create entertainment and distribute it on platforms like YouTube could also give rise to new media formats we haven't even imagined yet. So the question arises: who pays for the extra teachers, doctors, and nurses? His answer is that if AI truly generates such significant returns, the money will. be there. Part of the solution may involve how we tax labor versus capital . By aligning mechanisms, providing the right incentives, and having rational government channels, we can direct the productivity dividends created by AI into these sectors. But if it is not handled well, we will have to rely on robust institutional safety nets, which is fundamentally a matter of public administration. He made a very pragmatic point: if AI doesn't succeed, we won't even have the foundation to do these things, but in a world where AI is a huge success, there will be abundant funding for education and healthcare. He pointed out a scenario often overlooked : if everyone lets their own agent. compete for scarce resources, will the system get overwhelmed? Chatterjee gave an analogy: suppose everyone uses an agent to book the same popular restaurant, but the restaurant only has one phone line—it would ring incessantly . The solution is for the restaurant to also have an agent platform; both sides need platforms that can communicate with each other. In a future where everyone is competing for scarce resources, if there is an AI platform running on set rules to coordinate, the welfare benefits would be immense. He feels this is one of the most exciting, yet most overlooked, potentials of AI. He also specifically raised another perspective : people are always worried that AI will.

undermine the authority of human experts , which is a valid concern, but many overlook the scenario where AI acts as the first expert. If you cannot find a behavioral health specialist within 100 miles, you are already in a service desert; in this case, having an AI that can listen to you and offer initial advice is incredibly valuable. So, in many places where people have no resources to begin with, AI is actually filling that void. Finally, discussing exports and trade, Chatterjee said the lead department for economic policy has shifted; when he first joined the administration, this work was mostly in the Treasury and the White House, but over the last decade, the Commerce. Department has become a core player, or even the primary one. If an issue involves companies, AI adoption, or medium-sized businesses, you cannot bypass the Commerce Department; the host asked whether the goal for exporting US models over the next five years is to grow big or to leak those advantages. Chatterjee used an Economics 101 and 102 framework to answer this question. 101 argues that production should happen where costs are lowest and economies of scale are strongest. That is how global semiconductor manufacturing ended up highly concentrated in Taiwan, where TSMC is based. 102 argues that excessive concentration of production in one geographic region creates externalities ; if that region is also in a. geopolitically sensitive area, the externalities aren't just environmental or sustainability issues—they directly involve national security. Therefore, decision-making must be approached with the perspective of 102. Chatterjee’s own judgment is that access to models and intelligence will be important globally , but for frontier capabilities, especially in fields like cybersecurity , countries will be very cautious due to national interests, as power dynamics and security hinge on these things. Economic benefits and national security are, in reality, inseparable. This was also the biggest lesson he learned during his second stint in government. The first time he managed the economy, he barely dealt with national security. or defense officials. The second time he returned, almost everything had become geoeconomics, sitting at the intersection of national security and traditional economic policy. His generation of economists was not trained this way. He recalls asking a professor about industrial policy on his first day , only to be told that it was something for Europeans to worry about and the U.S. didn't need to bother. When he returned to government, he was racking his brain on how to rebuild a vibrant semiconductor manufacturing industry on U.S. soil. He believes this shift will span multiple sectors; AI, quantum computing, energy, and biology will all face the same issues. There is another change many people haven't realized: the. market logic of deep tech is different from the internet era. In the past, people were accustomed to using the global population to estimate the total addressable market. But once the market splits into several independent strategic camps, the math changes. The mission of the internet era was to bring more people in; the core problem for quantum computing is who breaks through first and whose technology is the strongest. When the underlying logic changes, the total market size changes too. So, how can an economist at a single company make people believe their research is neutral? Chad Syverson admits that he weighed the decision repeatedly before taking the job, because having worked in government, he knew that one's perspective shifts upon. entering the private sector. After taking office, he immediately realized that he had to bring in outside scholars . There are two reasons: first, academia can see things outside his field of vision. By opening a window for scholars under compliance and security frameworks , their insights can, in turn, inspire him. It’s impossible to have top experts in every niche field on the team, so leveraging external help is a must. They must publish publicly. The way economists communicate is through working papers and journals. Although those things sound old-fashioned, if you want to truly influence academia's understanding of AI, you have to write them. Even though the publication and.

review cycle for papers is long, once published, it lays a new layer of knowledge onto the entire discipline. He mentioned a working paper of his that was cited 850 times in less than a year , meaning 850 scholars believe this research is worth building upon. To put the outside world at ease, the team also did a few things. First, they made underlying data as public as possible so anyone wanting to run regressions or verify findings could do so. By going through rigorous peer review, having papers accepted by top journals at least shows that the broader academic community outside of the company also recognizes this rigor. Furthermore, they support others in conducting research rather than doing everything themselves. . They have a program called "Exchange, " which has funded 14 teams so far to conduct research using OpenAI's data with complete academic independence. The "Superalignment" team follows the same logic, with OpenAI bringing in Jason Furman and Michael Strain—one leaning left and the other right. His point is that even when economists have vastly different political stances, they still share a consensus on 85%of the fundamentals, with disagreements mainly centered on the frontier. In the future , billions of people will turn to AI every day for financial advice, news, and interpersonal relations; such a system must be neutral and evidence-based. Judgment criteria vary greatly among different people and. groups; only by inviting authorities from various schools of thought can trust be built. He specifically named Daron Acemoglu as the person he most wants to review OpenAI's data. This professor holds quite a few critical views on AI. While some might see that as dangerous, Zhatji’s attitude is quite the opposite, seeing it as motivation to identify and fill gaps. He is eager to share the underlying data with him without reservation and is curious to see if they will arrive at the same conclusions after the analysis. He expects there will still be differences in interpreting long-term trends, but when it comes to rigorous argumentation using solid data, Acemoglu is the ideal partner for debate. Of course, trust. cannot rely solely on high-level endorsements. He travels to many places to hold seminars and workshops, demonstrating in real-time what the AI outputs based on specific inputs. He said that while he used to be the teacher on the podium, through these visits, he has instead become the student. That is why he values face-to-face interaction so much; if you only argue on social media, it's easy to forget a basic truth, whereas when you are truly standing in front of someone, it is hard to be malicious. So, why doesn't this team conduct long-term forecasting? He said that trade-offs were necessary when building the team. They wanted to do everything at first, but experienced colleagues at OpenAI. advised him to cut some things back. The final principle decided upon was to focus on the present and focus on solid data. This also relates to his experience in government. Having sat in the seat of a policymaker, he knows that what officials and executives lack most isn't an imagination for 2035, but an understanding of what is happening right now. Long-term predictions can be overturned every six months, with implementation timelines constantly pushed back. Conversely, an empirical study that clearly explains how AI is impacting the job market right now is much more useful. Of course, there is a cost; upon release, the outside world might feel the conclusions offer nothing new, but before that, such intuition had. no data to back it up. In such a fast-changing era, making accurate predictions is difficult. While long-term forecasts expand our imagination, they also generate noise that can distract those who truly need to make decisions. Towards the end, the host asked him a rapid-fire question. What will the U.S. unemployment rate be by the end of 2030? He hopes for 5%or lower. When asked what the economy will be able to do in 2036 that it can't today, his answer was the emergence of truly intelligent organizations. Additionally, he checks one figure every week: revenue per employee. It's not for the entire industry, but for a group of companies he selected that have high AI.

exposure. Interestingly, he feels the hottest-growing industries aren't growing as fast as he thought, while some unassuming sectors are changing quietly. As for the two numbers mentioned at the beginning—10%growth and the unemployment rate tripling—those are exaggerated figures. His judgment is that it looks more like a slow wave. Although we don't see drastic changes in the short term, we know change is hidden within job boundaries, in the substance of organizational changes over four to five months, and in a productivity curve that hasn't turned yet. He says the road to AGI must pass through our organizations. Everyone is fixated on model capabilities, thinking that if it. can do something, it will be done, but they forget that for technology to be implemented, it must go through the organizational layer. So what we should really pay attention to might not be which benchmark scores a model just refreshed, but when your company integrates AI into real business processes and whether your own job boundaries have begun to expand. Thanks for watching, and see you next time.

  • 破除誇大迷思：由 OpenAI 首位首席經濟學家的權威視角，理性剖析 AI 帶來「10% 經濟暴衝」與「失業率短期暴增三倍」等不切實際的預測。
  • 揭示未來職場型態：探討未來工作者管理大量「AI Agent（代理人）」的全新組織模式，以及工作職責界線模糊化的核心趨勢。
  • 掌握全球與跨部門落地脈動：深入解析為何法務與人資是導入 AI 最快的黑馬部門，並對比日韓、東南亞、拉美與歐洲在 AI 普及上的顯著分歧。

摘要

破除 AI 經濟神話：理性看待成長與失業衝擊

作者大飛指出，圍繞當前 AI 熱潮的兩大極端預測——10% 的經濟成長率以及短期內失業率暴增三倍——在 OpenAI 首位首席經濟學家 Ronnie Chatterji 眼中均不切實際。Chatterji 認為，美國經濟只要增加 1% 至 2% 的成長率就已是翻天覆地的變革，而失業率哪怕僅微幅上升 0.5 到 1 個百分點，便足以引發嚴重的社會動盪；將 2020 年因疫情全面封城的極端經驗套用於未來 12 到 18 個月的 AI 衝擊，本質上是基準校準的錯誤。

從晶片法案到 OpenAI：首席經濟學家的職責與布局

曾深度參與美國《晶片法案》（CHIPS Act）推動的 Chatterji，在與 OpenAI 探討半導體議題的過程中，親手撰寫了首席經濟學家的職務描述，最終因緣際會親自接下該重任。他打造了一支融合經濟學博士、數據科學家與具備跨部門推進力的MBA 專案經理團隊。頂尖 AI 實驗室引進經濟學家的目的，除了將龐大的用戶數據解讀給商務部或各國央行等決策機構外，更關鍵的是研究未來工作者管理AI Agent（代理人）時，所催生出的全新組織行為與激勵機制。

未來 12 至 18 個月的趨勢：深層系統串接與職能界線模糊

展望未來一年半的局勢，Chatterji 提出三大核心觀察：第一，AI 革命才剛要深度滲透企業，關鍵在於跨出問答機器人形式，將連接器（Connectors）深度整合至現有企業系統中；第二，就業市場不會直接面臨全面淘汰，而是工作實質內容的轉變，許多員工已開始跨出既有職務描述，例如財務人員執行行銷任務、公關人員自主跑數據；第三，龐大的硬體資本支出已率先推動 GDP 數字，但實質的生產力躍升將在未來一年多內陸續浮現於統計數據中。

法務與人資的逆勢突圍與全球 AI 版圖的分歧

在企業內部落地節奏上，Chatterji 觀察到法務與人資部門因具備密集的流程與豐富的結構化數據，轉型速度出乎意料地名列前茅；以 OpenAI 內部為例，非技術部門全面深度整合 AI 僅比技術團隊落後約四至五個月。放大至全球格局，日本與南韓依託強大的晶片供應鏈與人口結構挑戰積極擁抱 AI；印尼與巴西則受惠於 18 至 25 歲的年輕人口紅利，展現超乎預期的活躍度；歐洲則深陷於科技自主架構與監管平衡的激烈辯論。為真實評測勞動力替代情況，OpenAI 亦推出依據美國勞工部 O*NET 架構的 JDBench 基準測試，藉由 44 種真實職業情境精準檢驗模型的實務能力。

As for the unemployment rate , even a rise of 0.5 to 1 percentage point is enough to trigger a serious social debate; it cannot happen silently . Regarding a tripling in the short term , he lived through 2020, when from the start of the year to April, the US unemployment rate tripled—but that was the result of the pandemic shutting down the entire economy. Why is he skeptical about using the same model to project. AI's impact over the next 12 to 18 months? That’s what we’re going to talk about today. Chatterji is OpenAI’s first chief economist, having been in the role for about two years. This position didn't actually exist at first; he had just finished his term in government, where he participated in the rollout of the CHIPS Act. He initially talked with OpenAI about chips and semiconductors. After several rounds of discussions and working with different groups of people , the topic shifted to a specific need: the company needed a chief economist. His response at the time was blunt: "I don't want the job, but I can help you write a job description." Later, when OpenAI came back to him with that job. description, seeing that they handed him the very document he had written, he realized he had the chance to shape the role exactly as he wanted. After consulting with his wife, he felt this was an opportunity he couldn't pass up. The job description was revised about six times, but two things never changed from the start. First, the research must be beneficial to people and provide the public with accurate information about AI. Because this position receives so much attention, anything released will surely be under intense scrutiny. Therefore, there is a responsibility to ensure that the outside world receives the right judgments. Second, there must be a team capable of delivering results. . He wants people with PhDs and data science backgrounds, but also people who are capable of driving things forward within the organization. Having worked in government, I know how hard it is to push things across departments, so I specifically recruited people with MBA backgrounds who have actually managed projects. In the end, this team was formed by a mix of project managers, data scientists, and economists. Tech companies hiring economists began roughly at the start of this century. When Hal Varian was still teaching at Berkeley, Chatterjee was his student and used his textbooks. Later, when Varian joined Google, the academic world was. shaken; back then, academics joining corporations was extremely rare. Later on, more and more economists entered tech firms. So why does a frontier lab need someone like this? The first reason is data. Beyond a handful of global institutions, we possess some of the richest data on AI usage in the consumer sector. This data needs to be interpreted and presented to institutions like the Department of Commerce or the Bank of England to help them understand what is happening in the industry. Although the company has a top-tier data science team, data scientists usually focus on product decisions; we need someone to step out.

of the lab and look at the broader socioeconomic structure. The second reason is even more novel: the company is creating a new class of economic participants. His hypothesis is that the next generation of workers will likely manage more AI agents than human colleagues. What exactly are the behavioral patterns of these agents? What kind of organizational structures will they spawn, and what incentive mechanisms should be used to regulate them? Economists have a ready-made toolkit for these questions. Looking at the next 12 to 18 months, he predicts three things will happen, and they are already emerging. First, the revolution will truly penetrate enterprises. He. says we are still at a very early stage . This might sound strange to say in San Francisco, but in the rest of the world , it is indeed just getting started. If we look at companies using AI now, the proportion that have truly enabled connectors to integrate AI into existing software is still very small. Yet this step is crucial; if AI doesn't have access to your computers and systems and is just a Q&A bot, its value clearly cannot be realized. Second, the job market won't change as drastically as many expect; what will change is the work content beneath the surface. He offered an observation: a large portion of work has already moved beyond job descriptions—for instance, finance. people are now handling marketing tasks , and corporate communications staff can run their own data. People are stepping outside their job boundaries to do things they’ve never done before. As more people in companies gain access to agents, this trend will only accelerate . Regarding productivity statistics, he said that AI has already entered GDP through capital expenditure, with hardware investment on a massive scale. However, economists are really eyeing productivity, and he expects more significant changes in this area over the next 12 to 18 months. As for the discussion about those two inflated numbers, they are essentially the same issue regarding our calibration of scale. . Moving on, the host asked a question that is easily overlooked: which department will actually make the first move? Chatterjee’s answer was somewhat counterintuitive. He said that legal and human resources—two departments many feel are far removed from AI—should not be underestimated. Within OpenAI, he observed the legal department transforming its workflow with AI as quickly as any team he has ever seen. He added a caveat that the legal profession itself is a biased sample and cannot fully represent the outside world. Regarding the pace of internal corporate adoption, using OpenAI as an example: in November 2025, various groups in San Francisco were having heated discussions. , with people sharing amazing use cases , but it wasn't until April and May 2026 that non-research and non-engineering departments became as deeply integrated with AI as the technical teams. He himself didn't fully start utilizing it until that time. According to him, as an economist with so many degrees who does data analysis every day, he is still classified as "non-technical" in the company system. Therefore, there is roughly a four to five-month lag between technical and non-technical departments . He emphasized that not every company is like OpenAI, but functions like legal and HR, which are process-intensive with abundant structured data, are what he. will be focusing on. The gap between enterprises is also widening. Some companies have already tapped into the potential of their internal super-users , while the so-called median adopters are still a long way from that step. This gap is not only widening, but it will also directly impact how much AI can be converted into economic results. When scaled to the national level, the divergence is even greater. Japan and South Korea are optimistic about AI's ability to transform the economy, driven by their past technological successes, demographics different from the West, and a group of companies that have already tasted the benefits. Looking at South Korea’s chip supply chain, with SK Hynix and Samsung leading the way, the effects are clearly visible. Enterprises.

in these regions are heavy users of AI, and because they were already connected to other technologies, the adoption of generative AI has been very smooth. A positive surprise is Indonesia and Brazil, where usage rates are much higher than he expected. Ou will release the relevant data, attributing a large part of the reason to a young population . People aged 18 to 25 are high-frequency AI users, a pattern seen globally. In Jakarta universities, he saw students discussing AI at a level almost identical to San Francisco, with no sense of lag. India is no longer a surprise; he attended an AI conference and was still deeply struck by the number of companies emerging around AI. More interesting are the large corporate groups. Having studied business school cases, they don't want to be the dinosaurs that get disrupted and are working hard to ensure they use AI. At the other end is Europe, where the struggle is two-fold: how to generate productivity from AI in enterprises, and how to safeguard core segments of their key tech stack amid globalization's retreat and shifting geopolitics. Since the Draghi memorandum was released, the internal debate in Europe has been intense. Chatterjee is reluctant to call it negative; he prefers to describe it as a genuine debate about what role AI should play in business and society. At. this point, the conversation shifted to a topic directly related to whether AI will take away jobs. OpenAI has created a benchmark test called JDBench. It doesn't use test questions, but instead uses real-world work to challenge the models. This is a test where experienced practitioners from 44 professions create questions and grade the models on whether they can do the job. The logic starts with a task list; the U.S. Department of Labor has a system called O*NET that breaks every profession down into individual tasks. With this list, one can ask: "Can AI do this task better than a human?" That is where the problem lies. Many people initially assume that. if a job has ten tasks and AI can do five of them better, then that person has a 50%chance of losing their job. But Chatterjee says that is not how things work at all. Chatterjee gave an example involving his own father. In 1984, his father installed a computer in his office. His father was an economics professor who needed to run large regressions. Before the computer, he had to carry stacks of punch cards into the machine room. Once broken down by task, the computer could do almost every part of the professor's job, but he didn't lose his job in 1984. He used the computer to run bigger regressions, build more models, and write more papers. . This example illustrates one thing: work being covered by AI does not mean being replaced by AI. Sometimes, it is quite the opposite; being covered means you have the opportunity to leverage it . Another reason less often mentioned is that tasks are endogenous; no one tells you to just do these ten things, as you have a higher goal, and tasks emerge to serve that objective. Satya's perspective on entrepreneurship is also related to his academic background. His doctoral dissertation studied entrepreneurship, which was not a mainstream topic at the time. Years later, seeing AI become another accelerator for startups and company. formation, he values the lessons of failure most; when he first started studying entrepreneurship, he thought the outcome was binary—either you build a company, or you end up with nothing. Later, after talking to those who had actually walked that path, he discovered that failure is often where one learns the most, and it can also be the prelude to the next great company. There are also some people who, only after starting a business, realize they are better suited as co-founders or simply working for someone else. Therefore, the faster the process, the better; one of the biggest benefits of AI is that it helps people reach that conclusion more quickly. This means there will be more failures, but fortunately, there will also be more successes, and the path for.

solo-entrepreneurship has been opened up . In many places, finding a co-founder is difficult, and hiring a Chief Marketing Officer is even harder; now these people can get started faster, leveraging an AI expert to gain knowledge that was previously out of reach. He feels this is a very tangible form of empowerment. Is this reflected in the data? The answer is yes. About half a year ago, a report was released showing that roughly 4 million Americans had used ChatGPT in some phase of starting a business. The aspect he values the most is brainstorming. He wrote a paper long ago on the startup process, which mentioned an incredible conclusion: the most common cause of. failure is actually the step of sharing the idea with others and getting feedback. Many people get stuck there, but now you can bypass that and directly ask AI for its take on the idea to get constructive feedback. Small businesses already in operation also benefit; restaurants can figure out which dishes should be on the menu, which sell well, and whether their selections are correct . These tasks used to require hiring expensive consultants, but now AI can provide a reasonably accurate answer. Returning to the macro level, has AI really entered the productivity data? His answer is divided into two parts. The first half is that AI is already reflected in GDP, and we must honestly. admit that. Looking at capital expenditure, 40 basis points to one percentage point of U.S. GDP growth can be attributed to AI infrastructure investment. It is not a small amount; it is a solid, genuine boost. And the second half of his point is that the next step is to convert this into productivity, or what economists call total factor productivity. He has seen that the data cited by Feynman aligns with the early emergence of AI effects, but it cannot be fully confirmed yet that AI is the cause; such verification often only happens in hindsight. He cited the famous 1995 Fed meeting where Alan Greenspan was convinced he saw productivity gains from technology,. while Janet Yellen said she hadn't seen it in the data yet. The final result was that the data was significantly revised upward later, so he judges that we might be at the beginning of that same moment , but it will take time before he can point to the data and say this is AI. He is confident in the market and in AI; business leaders are doubling down on investments and promoting them organization-wide, so they must be seeing returns, which will eventually translate into productivity. It just won't happen at all companies simultaneously, nor will it occur synchronously in every corner of the globe. He used that quote from William Gibson to summarize his answer: "The. future is already here—it's just not evenly distributed." As a joke, Gibson himself told friends he never actually said that, but he is quite happy to own it. So, if capital expenditure drives up demand and inflation, while productivity pulls inflation down, how will this tug-of-war play out? He says economists love this kind of game; inflation has many causes, and among the factors pushing it up today are the global situation, food prices, and a bunch of variables related to AI. The part related to AI depends on the hardware supply chain; for example, the price of DRAM memory has risen very sharply over. the past year. He believes that inflation caused by supply chain bottlenecks only accounts for a small piece, and as infrastructure expands and supply catches up, this part will gradually recede, which of course also depends on competition among companies in the chain. In the long run, it suppresses the force AI has to lower prices; it might not be visible within two years, but if we take a longer view , this deflationary effect will be significant. Some call this the "Jevons Paradox," but he prefers to call it a downward-sloping demand curve: if you lower the cost of completing a task, as long as there is enough elasticity, demand will rise, and many markets will expand as a result; he has already seen.

signs of this in his own research. If AI continues to deliver, what would it look like if we jumped straight to 2031? His approach is to look at countries first; the nations leading in adoption rates will reap the most dividends, and the United States is one of them. History will repeat itself, perhaps on an even larger scale. Stanford's Nick Bloom, John Van Reenen, and Raffaella Sadun famously analyzed IT adoption in US and UK firms. US firms had higher adoption rates and better management practices, leading to higher productivity—a dividend that boosted the US economy for. years. If the returns on AI are as expected, we will see a similar trajectory: US firms will fully embrace AI and use that capability globally to lift economic growth. An increase of one to two percentage points, or even three to four, would be a massive change. Looking at the employment structure, he predicts massive growth in education and healthcare. The logic is simple: the wealthier a society, the more it spends on education and healthcare. Once the AI dividend arrives, truly important priorities will emerge, with caring for people and educating the next generation at the forefront. Furthermore, history shows that when technology enters these. two fields, it often simultaneously creates a demand for more human labor. However, there is also a preference issue. He says if he had to choose between replacing a kindergarten teacher with a robot or shrinking class sizes so two teachers could instruct half the number of students, he would choose the latter. He believes most Americans feel the same regarding doctors, nurses, and caregivers. The real suspense lies in wages. Education and healthcare account for about one-seventh of US jobs. If we shift the economic focus to these areas but the new positions pay less than previous jobs, there is no gain—so. compensation for these roles must rise. The entertainment industry is another possible engine; he jokes about how many children now say they want to be influencers when they grow up. Economists love to track new job titles . It used to be cybersecurity experts; now it might be influencers. Even the term "podcaster" hasn't been around for very many years. Using AI and other tools to create entertainment and distribute it on platforms like YouTube could also give rise to new media formats we haven't even imagined yet. So the question arises: who pays for the extra teachers, doctors, and nurses? His answer is that if AI truly generates such significant returns, the money will. be there. Part of the solution may involve how we tax labor versus capital . By aligning mechanisms, providing the right incentives, and having rational government channels, we can direct the productivity dividends created by AI into these sectors. But if it is not handled well, we will have to rely on robust institutional safety nets, which is fundamentally a matter of public administration. He made a very pragmatic point: if AI doesn't succeed, we won't even have the foundation to do these things, but in a world where AI is a huge success, there will be abundant funding for education and healthcare. He pointed out a scenario often overlooked : if everyone lets their own agent. compete for scarce resources, will the system get overwhelmed? Chatterjee gave an analogy: suppose everyone uses an agent to book the same popular restaurant, but the restaurant only has one phone line—it would ring incessantly . The solution is for the restaurant to also have an agent platform; both sides need platforms that can communicate with each other. In a future where everyone is competing for scarce resources, if there is an AI platform running on set rules to coordinate, the welfare benefits would be immense. He feels this is one of the most exciting, yet most overlooked, potentials of AI. He also specifically raised another perspective : people are always worried that AI will.

undermine the authority of human experts , which is a valid concern, but many overlook the scenario where AI acts as the first expert. If you cannot find a behavioral health specialist within 100 miles, you are already in a service desert; in this case, having an AI that can listen to you and offer initial advice is incredibly valuable. So, in many places where people have no resources to begin with, AI is actually filling that void. Finally, discussing exports and trade, Chatterjee said the lead department for economic policy has shifted; when he first joined the administration, this work was mostly in the Treasury and the White House, but over the last decade, the Commerce. Department has become a core player, or even the primary one. If an issue involves companies, AI adoption, or medium-sized businesses, you cannot bypass the Commerce Department; the host asked whether the goal for exporting US models over the next five years is to grow big or to leak those advantages. Chatterjee used an Economics 101 and 102 framework to answer this question. 101 argues that production should happen where costs are lowest and economies of scale are strongest. That is how global semiconductor manufacturing ended up highly concentrated in Taiwan, where TSMC is based. 102 argues that excessive concentration of production in one geographic region creates externalities ; if that region is also in a. geopolitically sensitive area, the externalities aren't just environmental or sustainability issues—they directly involve national security. Therefore, decision-making must be approached with the perspective of 102. Chatterjee’s own judgment is that access to models and intelligence will be important globally , but for frontier capabilities, especially in fields like cybersecurity , countries will be very cautious due to national interests, as power dynamics and security hinge on these things. Economic benefits and national security are, in reality, inseparable. This was also the biggest lesson he learned during his second stint in government. The first time he managed the economy, he barely dealt with national security. or defense officials. The second time he returned, almost everything had become geoeconomics, sitting at the intersection of national security and traditional economic policy. His generation of economists was not trained this way. He recalls asking a professor about industrial policy on his first day , only to be told that it was something for Europeans to worry about and the U.S. didn't need to bother. When he returned to government, he was racking his brain on how to rebuild a vibrant semiconductor manufacturing industry on U.S. soil. He believes this shift will span multiple sectors; AI, quantum computing, energy, and biology will all face the same issues. There is another change many people haven't realized: the. market logic of deep tech is different from the internet era. In the past, people were accustomed to using the global population to estimate the total addressable market. But once the market splits into several independent strategic camps, the math changes. The mission of the internet era was to bring more people in; the core problem for quantum computing is who breaks through first and whose technology is the strongest. When the underlying logic changes, the total market size changes too. So, how can an economist at a single company make people believe their research is neutral? Chad Syverson admits that he weighed the decision repeatedly before taking the job, because having worked in government, he knew that one's perspective shifts upon. entering the private sector. After taking office, he immediately realized that he had to bring in outside scholars . There are two reasons: first, academia can see things outside his field of vision. By opening a window for scholars under compliance and security frameworks , their insights can, in turn, inspire him. It’s impossible to have top experts in every niche field on the team, so leveraging external help is a must. They must publish publicly. The way economists communicate is through working papers and journals. Although those things sound old-fashioned, if you want to truly influence academia's understanding of AI, you have to write them. Even though the publication and.

review cycle for papers is long, once published, it lays a new layer of knowledge onto the entire discipline. He mentioned a working paper of his that was cited 850 times in less than a year , meaning 850 scholars believe this research is worth building upon. To put the outside world at ease, the team also did a few things. First, they made underlying data as public as possible so anyone wanting to run regressions or verify findings could do so. By going through rigorous peer review, having papers accepted by top journals at least shows that the broader academic community outside of the company also recognizes this rigor. Furthermore, they support others in conducting research rather than doing everything themselves. . They have a program called "Exchange, " which has funded 14 teams so far to conduct research using OpenAI's data with complete academic independence. The "Superalignment" team follows the same logic, with OpenAI bringing in Jason Furman and Michael Strain—one leaning left and the other right. His point is that even when economists have vastly different political stances, they still share a consensus on 85%of the fundamentals, with disagreements mainly centered on the frontier. In the future , billions of people will turn to AI every day for financial advice, news, and interpersonal relations; such a system must be neutral and evidence-based. Judgment criteria vary greatly among different people and. groups; only by inviting authorities from various schools of thought can trust be built. He specifically named Daron Acemoglu as the person he most wants to review OpenAI's data. This professor holds quite a few critical views on AI. While some might see that as dangerous, Zhatji’s attitude is quite the opposite, seeing it as motivation to identify and fill gaps. He is eager to share the underlying data with him without reservation and is curious to see if they will arrive at the same conclusions after the analysis. He expects there will still be differences in interpreting long-term trends, but when it comes to rigorous argumentation using solid data, Acemoglu is the ideal partner for debate. Of course, trust. cannot rely solely on high-level endorsements. He travels to many places to hold seminars and workshops, demonstrating in real-time what the AI outputs based on specific inputs. He said that while he used to be the teacher on the podium, through these visits, he has instead become the student. That is why he values face-to-face interaction so much; if you only argue on social media, it's easy to forget a basic truth, whereas when you are truly standing in front of someone, it is hard to be malicious. So, why doesn't this team conduct long-term forecasting? He said that trade-offs were necessary when building the team. They wanted to do everything at first, but experienced colleagues at OpenAI. advised him to cut some things back. The final principle decided upon was to focus on the present and focus on solid data. This also relates to his experience in government. Having sat in the seat of a policymaker, he knows that what officials and executives lack most isn't an imagination for 2035, but an understanding of what is happening right now. Long-term predictions can be overturned every six months, with implementation timelines constantly pushed back. Conversely, an empirical study that clearly explains how AI is impacting the job market right now is much more useful. Of course, there is a cost; upon release, the outside world might feel the conclusions offer nothing new, but before that, such intuition had. no data to back it up. In such a fast-changing era, making accurate predictions is difficult. While long-term forecasts expand our imagination, they also generate noise that can distract those who truly need to make decisions. Towards the end, the host asked him a rapid-fire question. What will the U.S. unemployment rate be by the end of 2030? He hopes for 5%or lower. When asked what the economy will be able to do in 2036 that it can't today, his answer was the emergence of truly intelligent organizations. Additionally, he checks one figure every week: revenue per employee. It's not for the entire industry, but for a group of companies he selected that have high AI.

exposure. Interestingly, he feels the hottest-growing industries aren't growing as fast as he thought, while some unassuming sectors are changing quietly. As for the two numbers mentioned at the beginning—10%growth and the unemployment rate tripling—those are exaggerated figures. His judgment is that it looks more like a slow wave. Although we don't see drastic changes in the short term, we know change is hidden within job boundaries, in the substance of organizational changes over four to five months, and in a productivity curve that hasn't turned yet. He says the road to AGI must pass through our organizations. Everyone is fixated on model capabilities, thinking that if it. can do something, it will be done, but they forget that for technology to be implemented, it must go through the organizational layer. So what we should really pay attention to might not be which benchmark scores a model just refreshed, but when your company integrates AI into real business processes and whether your own job boundaries have begun to expand. Thanks for watching, and see you next time.

值得閱讀的理由

  • 破除誇大迷思：由 OpenAI 首位首席經濟學家的權威視角，理性剖析 AI 帶來「10% 經濟暴衝」與「失業率短期暴增三倍」等不切實際的預測。
  • 揭示未來職場型態：探討未來工作者管理大量「AI Agent（代理人）」的全新組織模式，以及工作職責界線模糊化的核心趨勢。
  • 掌握全球與跨部門落地脈動：深入解析為何法務與人資是導入 AI 最快的黑馬部門，並對比日韓、東南亞、拉美與歐洲在 AI 普及上的顯著分歧。

摘要

破除 AI 經濟神話：理性看待成長與失業衝擊

作者大飛指出，圍繞當前 AI 熱潮的兩大極端預測——10% 的經濟成長率以及短期內失業率暴增三倍——在 OpenAI 首位首席經濟學家 Ronnie Chatterji 眼中均不切實際。Chatterji 認為，美國經濟只要增加 1% 至 2% 的成長率就已是翻天覆地的變革，而失業率哪怕僅微幅上升 0.5 到 1 個百分點，便足以引發嚴重的社會動盪；將 2020 年因疫情全面封城的極端經驗套用於未來 12 到 18 個月的 AI 衝擊，本質上是基準校準的錯誤。

從晶片法案到 OpenAI：首席經濟學家的職責與布局

曾深度參與美國《晶片法案》（CHIPS Act）推動的 Chatterji，在與 OpenAI 探討半導體議題的過程中，親手撰寫了首席經濟學家的職務描述，最終因緣際會親自接下該重任。他打造了一支融合經濟學博士、數據科學家與具備跨部門推進力的MBA 專案經理團隊。頂尖 AI 實驗室引進經濟學家的目的，除了將龐大的用戶數據解讀給商務部或各國央行等決策機構外，更關鍵的是研究未來工作者管理AI Agent（代理人）時，所催生出的全新組織行為與激勵機制。

未來 12 至 18 個月的趨勢：深層系統串接與職能界線模糊

展望未來一年半的局勢，Chatterji 提出三大核心觀察：第一，AI 革命才剛要深度滲透企業，關鍵在於跨出問答機器人形式，將連接器（Connectors）深度整合至現有企業系統中；第二，就業市場不會直接面臨全面淘汰，而是工作實質內容的轉變，許多員工已開始跨出既有職務描述，例如財務人員執行行銷任務、公關人員自主跑數據；第三，龐大的硬體資本支出已率先推動 GDP 數字，但實質的生產力躍升將在未來一年多內陸續浮現於統計數據中。

法務與人資的逆勢突圍與全球 AI 版圖的分歧
